The chapter repeats, as narrative, instructions already given as command, and three of the witnesses take the repetition itself as the thing to be explained. Henry raises the objection first and at length: Moses had already recorded the instructions given on the mount, and it might have sufficed to say in a few words that each thing was made according to those directions. Since scripture contains no idle words and no vain repetitions, the chapters cannot be needless, however tedious they seem. His answer is that Moses wrote first for Israel, who were never admitted to see the furniture of the tabernacle — only the priests were — so what they could not look at had to be described to them at length; and that what we ought to read again is written again, as the same passages of the history of Christ are related by two or three and some by four of the evangelists. Wesley keeps both halves of that argument almost word for word, adding that Moses thereby appeals to every reader concerning his fidelity to him that appointed him, and teaches us to have respect to all God’s commandments, even to every jot and tittle.

Calvin answers the same objection from the other end. The Holy Spirit narrates the execution in almost the identical words in which he had set out the command, so that we may understand that neither Moses nor the artificers varied in the smallest point from the rule prescribed. God commanded the ark and its cover, and Moses relates it completed without the omission of a minute detail; he ordered the table, and not a syllable is neglected; the candlestick, the altar of incense and the composition of the oil answer the command exactly. From this Calvin draws the chapter’s doctrine: Moses is commending obedience as the foundation of true piety, and reminding us that there was no exercise of the imagination anywhere in the service of the tabernacle, since nothing is more opposed to the purity of religion than doing what is not enjoined.

The remaining question is why the work is credited to one man. Gill reports that Jarchi explained the naming from Bezaleel’s having given his mind to this work more than the rest of the wise men, and that some Jewish writers held he made the ark without help — a notion Gill rejects, since the mercy seat, the cherubim, the shewbread table, the candlestick, the two altars and the laver of brass are all ascribed to him in the same way. They are said to be made by him because they were made by his direction and under his oversight; and Gill takes from Aben Ezra the further point that the singular ascription is made here particularly for the glory of the ark. Ellicott narrows the credit from the other side, noting that Aholiab had no part in constructing the furniture of the tabernacle at all, but only in the coverings, the veil, the curtains and the priests’ dresses, and referring to Exodus 38:23 for it.

Wesley alone reads the three objects of these verses as a single figure. Taking the ark with the mercy seat and the cherubim together, he finds in them the glory of a holy God, the sincerity of a holy heart, and the communion between them by a Mediator: it is God’s glory that he dwells between the cherubim, continually attended by the blessed angels, whose swiftness the wings signify and whose unanimity in service is signified by their faces being one toward another; it is the character of an upright heart that, like the ark of the testimony, it has the law of God hid and kept within it; and by Christ the great propitiation a reconciliation is made, since he interposes between us and God’s displeasure.
10:
Henry reads the table of shewbread as a statement about God’s housekeeping. God is a good householder who keeps a plentiful table: if the world is his tabernacle, his providence spreads one for all the creatures; if the church is, his grace spreads one for believers, furnished with the bread of life. But he will not leave the two dispensations level. The table here was furnished only with shew-bread, to be looked upon and not fed upon while it stood there, and eaten afterwards by the priests alone; whereas to the table Christ has spread in the new covenant all real Christians are invited guests, and to them it is said, Eat, O friends, come eat of my bread. What the law gave only a sight of at a distance, the gospel gives the enjoyment of, and a hearty welcome to.

The candlestick he treats by its material. It was not wood overlaid with gold but all beaten work of pure gold, signifying the light of divine revelation by which God’s church on earth has always been enlightened, supplied continually with fresh oil from Christ the good Olive (Zechariah 4:2-3). Even so, God’s manifestations of himself in this world are only candle-light compared with the daylight of the future state. The Bible is that golden candlestick, pure gold (Psalm 19:10), diffusing light to every part of the tabernacle so that God’s spiritual priests may see to minister and to do the service of the sanctuary. Henry then takes up ornament: the candlestick had not only bowls for use but knops and flowers for beauty, and God has adorned his word with many things for which we can give no more reason than for these — yet may be sure they were added for a good purpose. His conclusion is practical: bless God for the candlestick, keep an eye to it continually, and dread its removal out of its place.

Wesley adds nothing here that Henry has not already said. His note repeats the contrast between the dispensations in almost the same words, down to the invitation and the closing observation that what the law gave a sight of at a distance the gospel gives the enjoyment of.
